b: p
I appear to be the victim of stealth lifestyle creep.
p

I'm on vacation with family and friends, celebrating my wife's birthday. To keep costs reasonable for everyone else, we booked a competitively priced complex of Mediterranean-style, two-bedroom apartments with little garden patios, arranged around an enormous pool and sun deck with a basic bar and restaurant attached.
p

Visually, it's lovely. The two-story apartments are painted in classic Mediterranean style, and winding paths cut through lush grass beneath tall palms rustling in the sea breeze. And yet, I'm embarrassed to admit, I find it somewhat wanting.
p
First-world problems, I know. The layout is awkward. I've already bumped my head several times grabbing things from the fridge, which is wedged under the stairwell like an afterthought.
p

There's barely any closet space, the mattress and bedding are merely so-so, and the bathroom has a geometry Euclid would have disowned. The toilet paper is questionable, and the A/C works, though it wheezes like an asthmatic.
p

Meanwhile, everyone else in our group is thrilled with the place. I'm keeping my mouth firmly shut about the room. I think I would be judged if I suggested the place is a little frayed around the edges.
p
I have, however, found myself gently lobbying everyone to venture out hunting down decent restaurants rather than settling for the on-site burgers, fries and pizza.
p
This is the same guy who once spent three months backpacking through Southeast Asia and Australia with three pairs of underwear to his name. When on earth did this happen to me?
p

The honest answer is that it probably happened years ago, one small upgrade at a time. I just didn't notice until a fridge started assaulting me. I like to imagine my backpacking self, sunburnt, broke and delighted with a plastic chair, putting me on trial. He'd call the fridge as his first witness, and the mattress as his second.
p

My defense is simple: with age, thread count and sensible sight lines in the bathroom stop being luxuries and start being infrastructure. At twenty-three, I could sleep on a bus luggage rack and wake up refreshed. Now I wake up negotiating with my own lumbar region. The defense rests, preferably on something with a decent thread count.
p

So I'll put it to the jury: what would your younger self say if they saw how you travel now, and would you win the argument? What's the one upgrade you now consider infrastructure rather than luxury? I'll be here, putting on a crash helmet before approaching the fridge, awaiting your verdict.
